description: Toy Box Friends G5-03: volume as unit cubes in layers, V = l × w × h = B × h, joined boxes add, and 1,000 cm³ = 1 L, in a box factory.

youtube.title: Volume for Kids: Length × Width × Height and Unit Cubes | Grade 5 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
A tall box and a wide box: which holds more cubes? At the Box Factory, Robo, Monkey and Penguin fill boxes layer by layer, lift the layers apart to find the hidden cubes, and discover the volume formula.
You'll learn: volume is the number of unit cubes that fill a solid (cubic centimeters, cm³), one layer × the number of layers, V = l × w × h = B × h, adding the volumes of joined boxes, and 1,000 cm³ = 1 liter (1 cm³ = 1 mL).
Try at home: build boxes from blocks or dice and count the layers. Small cubes are a choking risk: keep them away from babies and toddlers.

do.text: Volume Box Factory
Welcome to the Box Factory! Two new boxes. The sign says: fill me with cubes!
The tall one holds way more. It's huge!
Which box holds more cubes? What do you think?
Let's fill them and count.
The wide box holds twenty-four cubes. The tall box holds... twenty-four!
No way! They hold the same?
Volume is how much space something takes up. We measure it with cubes.
volume
Here's a flat square, one centimeter on each side. It covers area.
Here's a cube, one centimeter on every edge. It takes up space.
Area counts squares on a flat surface. Volume counts the cubes that fill a solid.
This cube is one cubic centimeter. We write it c m with a little three.
Our cubes look bigger than one centimeter!
Good eye! We drew them bigger so you can count them.
drawn bigger
Try this small box: two cubes long, two wide and two high. How many cubes fill it?
Four on the bottom, four on top: eight cubes!
Yes. Its volume is eight cubic centimeters.
The wide box is four cubes long and three cubes wide.
Let's fill the bottom layer, row by row.
Four times three: twelve cubes in one layer.
The box is two cubes high, so we stack a second layer: twelve more.
Twelve plus twelve is twenty-four cubes.
Wait, I only count eighteen! Front, top and side.
How many cubes are hiding where you can't see them?
Let's lift the top layer, like a cake.
Look at the bottom layer. Six cubes were hiding at the back and in the middle.
Eighteen plus six hidden cubes is twenty-four. I'll never forget the hidden ones!
Let's practice. This box is three long, two wide and three high. Count in layers.
How many cubes in one layer? And how many layers?
Three times two is six in a layer. Three layers: eighteen!
Let's find a shortcut. Length four, width three, height two.
The base is the bottom layer. Its area, B, is length times width: twelve.
base area
The height tells how many layers. Volume is B times h: twelve times two.
height
That's the same as length times width times height.
One layer?
Length times width!
How many layers?
The height!
Now the tall box: two by two by six. The base is four cubes.
Six layers of four: twenty-four cubic centimeters.
Same volume, different shape. So tall doesn't mean more!
I'll write it down: twenty-four square centimeters!
Careful! Square centimeters are for flat area. Volume uses cubic centimeters.
Cubes for volume. Little three, not little two!
Can you make other boxes from twenty-four cubes?
Two by three by four.
One by four by six.
Two by two by six.
And a tower: one by three by eight!
Different shapes, but every one is twenty-four cubic centimeters.
Check one: two times three is six, times four is twenty-four.
Like cereal boxes! Some are tall and thin, some are short and wide.
Exactly. To compare, don't just look at height. Count the cubes, or multiply.
This shape is made of two boxes. How can we find its volume?
Way one: split it flat. The bottom box is four by three by two: twenty-four.
The top box is two by three by two: twelve. Twenty-four plus twelve is thirty-six.
Way two: split it the other way. A tall column and a short box.
Two by three by four is twenty-four. Two by three by two is twelve.
Thirty-six again! However you split it, the volumes add up.
Which split would you choose? Either way works, so pick the one that's easiest to multiply.
Volumes of joined boxes add.
Now a big one: ten by ten by ten.
That's one thousand cubic centimeters.
Here's a hollow box the same size. Will one liter of juice fill it?
Let's pour and see! One liter carton.
It fills it exactly! One thousand cubic centimeters is one liter.
So one cubic centimeter is one milliliter.
1 cm³ = 1 mL
So a one-liter milk carton holds one thousand cubic centimeters too!
Fun fact: the liter was first defined as the space inside a cube ten centimeters on each side.
A fish tank is thirty by twenty by twenty centimeters. How much water?
Twelve thousand cubic centimeters: that's twelve liters.
And an Olympic pool holds about two and a half million liters!
Length times width makes a layer!
Stack them high, the height's the player!
One layer?
Length times width!
How many layers?
The height!
All together: length times width makes a layer, stack them high, the height's the player!
I'm the shipping clerk. Three orders to pack!
Order one: a box five by four by three centimeters. What's its volume?
Five times four is twenty. Twenty times three is sixty cubic centimeters.
Order two: a four by three base must hold forty-eight. How tall?
One layer is twelve. Forty-eight divided by twelve is four layers. Four centimeters tall!
Order three: double the height of a two by three by four box. What happens?
Two by three by eight is forty-eight. Double the height, double the volume!
Check: four by three by four is forty-eight. It fits!
All orders shipped!
Question one. A box is three by four by five centimeters. What is its volume?
Sixty cubic centimeters.
Question two. Why did Monkey count eighteen instead of twenty-four?
He missed the six hidden cubes inside and at the back.
Question three. How many cubic centimeters are in two liters?
Two thousand cubic centimeters.
Question four. A twenty-four box joins a twelve box. What's the volume?
Thirty-six cubic centimeters.
Let's recap. Volume counts cubes: one layer times the number of layers.
V equals l times w times h. Joined boxes add. And one thousand cubic centimeters is one liter.
And always look for the hidden cubes!
Your turn! Use building blocks or dice. Build a box three long, two wide and two high.
count the layers
Predict the count first, then build and check. Can you make three boxes of twelve?
Small cubes are a choking risk, so keep them away from babies. See you next time!
